## The question

30 Doradus is the most active star-forming region in the Local Group. It is
also full of dust, and dust is a problem: it absorbs and scatters starlight,
preferentially at short wavelengths, so every measurement made through it comes
out dimmer and redder than the truth. Before you can say anything about the
physical conditions inside the nebula, you have to know how much dust you are
looking through — and that number changes from one line of sight to the next.

The goal of this project is a **spatially resolved extinction map**: a value of
$\ebv$ at every position across the region, derived from the data itself rather
than assumed.

## Why Balmer decrements work

Hydrogen recombination fixes the intrinsic ratio of $\halpha$ to $\hbeta$. Under
Case B recombination at $T_e \approx 10^4\ \mathrm{K}$ and
$n_e \approx 10^2\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, that ratio is

$$
\left(\frac{F_{\halpha}}{F_{\hbeta}}\right)_{\text{intrinsic}} \approx 2.86 .
$$

Because the ratio is set by atomic physics, any departure from it is telling us
about the path, not the source. Dust reddens the light, so the observed ratio
comes out larger. The colour excess follows directly:

$$
\ebv = \frac{2.5}{k(\lambda_{\hbeta}) - k(\lambda_{\halpha})}
       \log_{10}\!\left[
         \frac{(F_{\halpha}/F_{\hbeta})_{\text{observed}}}{2.86}
       \right],
$$

where $k(\lambda)$ is the assumed extinction curve. Do this once and you have a
number. Do it at every spaxel in an IFU cube and you have a map.
